title: What is & How to Do Tabulation
description: Build DP answers bottom-up by filling a table from the base cases

sections.title: 3. How to Build a Tabulation Solution
5. Memoization vs Tabulation: Which to Use
6. How to Approach a Problem with Tabulation

blocks.text: Tabulation is the other main way to write dynamic programming. Instead of recursing from the big problem down, you start from the smallest subproblems and build up to the answer, filling a table as you go.
Because it starts small and grows, tabulation is called the bottom-up approach. There is no recursion at all, just loops.

In tabulation you create a table, usually an array, where each cell holds the answer to one subproblem. You fill it in an order that guarantees every value you need is already computed before you use it.
The final answer is simply one of the cells in the table, typically the last one you fill.

items: Create a table indexed by subproblem
Fill in the base cases directly
Fill the rest in dependency order using earlier cells
Read the answer out of the table

blocks.text: Memoization and tabulation compute the same values, just in opposite directions.

blocks.caption: Top-down starts at n and recurses down; bottom-up starts at the base cases and builds up

blocks.text: Top-down (memoization) starts at the big problem and dives toward the base cases, caching along the way. Bottom-up (tabulation) starts at the base cases and climbs toward the big problem with plain loops.

content.title: 3. How to Build a Tabulation Solution

blocks.text: Converting a recurrence into a table follows a reliable recipe.

items: Define what each table cell means, for example dp[i] is the answer for input i.
Fill the base cases the recurrence starts from.
Find the iteration order so every dependency is ready before it is used.
Translate the recurrence into an assignment inside the loop.
Return the cell that represents the full problem.

blocks.caption: Fill the table left to right, each cell built from the two before it
blocks.alt: How to Build a Tabulation Solution

blocks.text: The single most important part of tabulation is the order in which you fill the table. A cell can only be computed after everything it depends on already exists.

For 1D problems this is usually a simple left to right loop. For 2D grids you often go row by row. For interval problems you loop by increasing interval length. Always trace one cell and check its dependencies are already filled.

The order rule:

Ask: "which cells does dp[i] read?" Then choose a loop order that fills all of those before dp[i]. Get this wrong and you read empty cells.

content.title: 5. Memoization vs Tabulation: Which to Use

blocks.text: Both are correct dynamic programming. The choice comes down to trade-offs.

items: Tabulation avoids recursion, so no stack overflow, and it is often a bit faster with less overhead.
Memoization is easier to write from a recurrence and only computes the states you actually reach.
Tabulation computes every cell, which can waste work if many states are never needed.
Space optimization is usually easier to spot in tabulation, since the fill order is explicit.

blocks.text: A common workflow is to prototype with memoization to confirm correctness, then rewrite as tabulation when you want speed or need to optimise space.

content.title: 6. How to Approach a Problem with Tabulation

blocks.text: When you are ready to write bottom-up, work through this.

items: State clearly what one table cell represents.
Write the base cases directly into the table.
Determine the fill order from the dependencies.
Loop and apply the recurrence as an assignment.
Return the cell for the whole problem, then consider trimming space.

blocks.text: Once your table fills cleanly and the answer is correct, you are usually one small step away from a space optimized solution.
